extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, extramural investigators, and PIs (especially those writing R01/resubmission applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for preparing, revising, and understanding review of NIH extramural grant applications (R01-scale), including resubmissions, budgeting, and reviewer behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Published vs not-published preliminary data
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion of relevant data that are published is viewed as a strength and the lack thereof as a weakness; reviewers may laud the provision of supportive preliminary data and criticize the lack of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is 'completely fair and consistent with a long history of NIH study section behavior.' Treat inclusion of published preliminary data as a verifiable strength; absence will repeatedly be cited as weakness. But adding such data does not guarantee funding because reviewers form overall positions that may still find other weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint vs peer-reviewed publication status
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may treat preprints as weaker evidence than peer-reviewed publications; comments can escalate from 'not published' → 'preprint' → 'peer-reviewed journal'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some reviewers legitimately view peer review acceptance as superior. Depositing a preprint may help, but some reviewers will still prefer peer-reviewed articles. You can disagree with this assessment, but it is within accepted review practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact factor (JIF) as proxy for publication quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may treat publication in a higher JIF journal as a superior strength and publication in a low JIF journal as less supportive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JIF is an objective/verifiable shorthand reviewers use. Don't be surprised if reviewers cite JIF differences as evidence for or against productivity/preliminary data value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Stock Critiques (verifiable shorthand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers deploy conventional, objectively verifiable critiques (e.g., presence/absence of preliminary data, publication status, JIF) as convenient shorthands for arguing a grant should/should not be funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stock critiques are efficient and persuasive in panel communication; they are easier to use than nuanced methodological debates. Expect reviewers to use them to justify overall impact positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall impact driven by reviewer gestalt/choice, not strictly by Approach fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers usually form an overall impact position (a general 'fund it'/'don't fund it' stance) and then write strength/weakness bullets that confirm that position rather than produce an objective post-hoc summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixing all weaknesses in Approach does not reliably change overall impact because reviewers may still 'choose to find other weaknesses.' The application as a whole, and having assigned reviewer advocates, matter more than any single element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of Approach criterion with overall impact (and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH data show overall impact votes were best correlated with Approach criterion scores, but this correlation can mislead applicants into over-focusing on writing a 'perfect' Approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Approach scores correlate with overall impact, the causality is not straightforward; reviewers' pre-existing overall positions and whether they 'get' the big-picture idea can drive both Approach and overall scores. Don't assume a perfect Approach guarantees fundable score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / Innovation / Investigator / Environment criteria context
rubrics_metrics.description: The five standard NIH review criteria (Significance, Investigator, Innovation, Approach, Environment) are co-equal in theory but behave differently in practice depending on reviewers' judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaknesses can be framed in any of these categories. Reviewers may emphasize Significance (importance of the question) or Investigator (productivity/expertise) when assigning strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for assigned reviewer advocates
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant needs advocates among the assigned reviewers (the three assigned reviewers) who broadly support the big-picture importance of the proposal — these advocates can overlook Approach weaknesses and drive favorable scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Securing reviewers who 'get it' is crucial; assigned reviewers' overall stance signals to Program and to the panel. You cannot reliably predict who will be advocates; the same roster can include people who help or hinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resubmission Introduction requirements and marking-changes prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Introduction to a Resubmission must include a summary of substantial additions, deletions, and changes and a response to weaknesses raised in the Summary Statement; NIH NOT-OD-24-061 states markups (bracketing, bolding, highlighting, margin lines, typography changes, etc.) should not be used to identify changes in Resubmission applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There has been confusion between earlier permissive practice and the current guidance. Do not use markups to indicate changes; instead include a concise one-page Introduction describing changes and responses. Consider adding a statement in the Introduction noting that changes are not marked per current NIH policy to avoid reviewer confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to prior reviewer critiques (strategy and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmissions are expected to respond to prior criticisms, but addressing some criticisms can create new issues or introduce fresh fodder for weakness bullets; there is no way to make a proposal entirely immune from critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the most important critiques given limited page space; be strategic whether to adopt suggested experimental variants (which can trade off expertise/preliminary data). Recognize you cannot be perfect; balance rebuttal vs. revision risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility as determinant for reviewer invitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and SROs recruit reviewers based on visibility—publishing in the subfield, presenting at meetings, being known to peers—so lack of visibility reduces invitations to review manuscripts and grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be invited as a reviewer (which can benefit career visibility), inhabit a subfield: publish in it, attend conferences, present posters, join societies. Visibility increases likelihood of being asked to review and to serve on study sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic budgeting and expectation of NIH budget cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH routinely cuts proposed budgets; ICs may reduce award levels, reduce years of funding, or apply across-the-board reductions (especially under Continuing Resolutions). Reviewers may recommend reductions in personnel effort rather than dollar amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for rebudgeting or scope reduction; don't assume NOA will match your proposed budget. Reviewers' suggested cuts (e.g., reduce postdoc effort) are common; NIH NOAs typically state the awarded total and PIs can rebudget within limits but risk PO disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: IC-specific policies and funding behavior matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutes/Centers (ICs) differ in policies (e.g., NIAMS limiting PIs with >=3 R01-equivalent awards to low program priority) and in conservative behavior under Continuing Resolutions, affecting funding likelihood independent of grant quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know IC-specific notices (e.g., NOT-AR-24-013) and how they define R01-equivalent awards and exceptions. Consider strategic budgeting and proposal timing given IC tendencies; policies can force changes in applicant strategy (e.g., proposing higher-dollar R01s to maximize limited award slots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock reviewer behaviors: confirmatory writing and choosing weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers often write strengths/weaknesses as 'an exercise in confirming an overall impact position' and can choose to overlook or emphasize particular weaknesses depending on their overall stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect confirmatory critiques; multiple reviewers may triangulate to justify a final score. Understand that reviewers can and will 'find other weaknesses' if their overall position isn't changed by your revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time investment realities for R01 preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims such as '200 hours to prepare an R01' are contested; first R01s may take much longer, subsequent ones may be faster due to reuse of materials; unrealistic time expectations can be harmful for early-career PIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan workload realistically; leverage prior proposals and templates to reduce time. Recognize that extremely high per-proposal time budgets (if true) make sustaining multiple submissions per year impractical for new PIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program-level funding considerations (Program/PO decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmatic decisions (Program/PO) and IC priorities (e.g., NOSIs, NOSIs' opaque influence) affect funding beyond peer review scores; Program can use routing boxes (Box 4B) and NOSIs to prioritize certain proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with Program Officers to understand IC priorities and NOSIs. Don’t assume peer review score alone ensures funding; Program-level portfolio balancing and set-asides affect final awards.
